strengths: The paper addresses an important and underexplored reliability concern for MLLM-based chart understanding: robustness to misleading visualizations, with clear societal relevance (disinformation).

The evaluation is broad and reasonably rigorous: 18 MLLMs spanning open-weight, commercial, and chart-specialized models; three datasets covering synthetic and real-world misleading cases plus ChartQA; comparisons against random baselines and reported human accuracy.
The paper introduces a new resource: 42 real-world misleading visualizations annotated with misleader types and paired with MCQs, filling a gap in prior synthetic-only benchmarks.

Experiment 3 evaluates six inference-time correction methods with proper statistical testing (McNemar) and, importantly, analyzes the trade-off between improving accuracy on misleading visualizations and preserving accuracy on non-misleading ones, an aspect the authors plausibly claim prior/parallel work ignores.

The analysis goes beyond aggregate scores: per-misleader breakdowns (Figure 5), Likert-consistency testing (Experiment 2), a qualitative analysis of table extraction failures (Figure 8), and honest discussion of when warning-based methods are impractical.
The study is transparent about limitations (map support, chart-type assumptions, misleader imbalance) and releases code and data, supporting reproducibility.

The related work positioning is careful, distinguishing the contribution from concurrent benchmarking efforts (Bendeck and Stasko, 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Pandey and Ottley, 2025; Valentim et al., 2025).
weaknesses: Statistical power is limited in places: Experiment 2 relies on only 4 visualization pairs with a t-test; several misleader categories contain n=1-3 instances (overplotting, missing data, inappropriate use of pie chart), making per-misleader accuracy estimates highly unstable and the 'worst performers at 0%' claims fragile.

There are potential confounds when comparing accuracy across misleading vs. non-misleading datasets: the datasets differ in question type distribution, chart complexity, and provenance, so the accuracy drop may partially reflect dataset difficulty rather than misleaders alone. The paper does not fully control for or discuss this.

Experiment 3 (the mitigation contribution) is evaluated on only three mid-sized open-weight models; it is unclear whether the conclusions (e.g., table-based QA trade-offs) generalize to larger or commercial models.

The effectiveness of table-based QA hinges on table extraction quality, which cannot be directly evaluated without ground-truth tables; the indirect CHARTOM analysis (7.1% perfect match) is suggestive but the impact of extraction errors on the reported gains is not quantified.

The new 42-instance real-world dataset is modest in size and its MCQs are manually created by the authors without reported inter-annotator agreement or validation procedures, raising questions about annotation quality and potential bias toward the paper's hypotheses.

The headline claim of being 'the first' comprehensive study and first to propose correction methods is weakened by acknowledged parallel works; the correction methods themselves (warning prompts, table extraction, code-based redrawing) are relatively straightforward engineering choices rather than novel techniques.

The finding that the real-world subset shows higher accuracy due to parametric knowledge is acknowledged as a caveat but complicates the central vulnerability narrative; the paper could better quantify this effect (e.g., by testing questions about post-cutoff data).

Some methodological details are underspecified for full reproducibility, e.g., how free-text answers on ChartQA and CHARTOM are scored, and how the random baseline of 25.6% is computed across heterogeneous question formats.

strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: the vulnerability of MLLMs to misleading visualizations is directly relevant to reliable chart QA and disinformation concerns, and the paper is positioned relative to the visualization-literature taxonomies.

Broad empirical coverage: Experiment 1 evaluates 18 MLLMs (open-weight, commercial, and chart-specialized) across 143 misleading and 124 non-misleading instances covering 17 misleader types, plus ChartQA, with per-misleader breakdowns (Figure 5).
A new dataset of 42 real-world misleading visualizations with manually created MCQs is introduced, complementing the synthetic CALVI/CHARTOM data and probing parametric-knowledge shortcuts.

Experiment 2 tests a complementary notion of vulnerability (consistency across misleading/non-misleading versions of the same data), with significance testing, which strengthens the claim beyond aggregate accuracy.

The mitigation study is framed with a sensible goal (improve misleading-chart QA without degrading non-misleading accuracy) and includes statistical testing (McNemar), an analysis of the table-extraction bottleneck (Figure 8), and honest reporting of trade-offs (table-based QA costs up to 8.5 pp on non-misleading charts).
Code and data are made available, and implementation details (seed, temperature, zero-shot prompting, model access) support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Scale of the core evaluation is small: 143 misleading instances (with 42 in the real-world subset, 12 misleader types represented by <=9 instances, several by a single instance) and only 4 visualization pairs in Experiment 2, so per-category and consistency conclusions rest on very few items and noisy estimates.

Correction methods (Experiment 3) are evaluated on only three mid-sized open-weight models, which limits the generality of the findings about what works and why; no commercial model is included despite it being central to Experiment 1.

Comparability across question types is a concern: MCQ, free-text, and rank questions are pooled into one 'accuracy', and the random baseline (25.6%) is only defined for MCQ; the effect sizes may partly reflect format differences rather than the misleaders themselves.

Several methods rely on assumptions (ground-truth misleader labels for warnings, known chart type, successful table extraction) whose failure modes are acknowledged but not fully quantified; the warning method is effectively shown unpromising, and its inclusion adds length without much insight.

Novelty is moderated by acknowledged parallel work (Chen et al., 2025; Pandey and Ottley, 2025; Valentim et al., 2025; Bendeck and Stasko, 2025) reporting similar MLLM vulnerabilities; the clearest original contributions are the real-world subset and the correction-method comparison, but the latter is largely prompt-based engineering whose best method (table-based QA) essentially bypasses the visualization.

Table extraction quality, the linchpin of both effective methods, cannot be directly evaluated (no ground-truth tables), leaving the mechanism behind the trade-offs partly speculative ('we make the hypothesis that...').
Some figures (4, 5, 7) are dense bar charts that are difficult to read precisely; aggregate claims in text would benefit from accompanying tables in the appendix.

strengths: Important and timely problem: robustness of MLLMs to misleading visualizations is largely unexplored in chart-understanding research, and the paper makes a convincing case for its societal relevance (disinformation).

Breadth of evaluation: 18 MLLMs spanning open-weight, commercial, and chart-specialized models, with 17 misleader types; the per-misleader analysis (Figure 5) yields genuinely interesting findings, e.g., area encoding deceives MLLMs but not humans, while dual axes deceive humans more than MLLMs.

New real-world dataset of 42 annotated misleading visualizations with manually created MCQs, complementing existing synthetic resources (CALVI, CHARTOM) and enabling analysis under parametric-knowledge conflict; code and data are released, supporting reproducibility.

Correction-method study is well designed around the practical trade-off: improving accuracy on misleading charts without degrading non-misleading performance, an aspect the authors correctly note prior parallel work does not address.

Statistical rigor is present where it matters: McNemar tests for correction-method deltas, paired t-tests for Likert consistency, and honest reporting that several methods (warnings, axes) do not help, including that table-based QA hurts non-misleading accuracy for some models.
The table-extraction analysis (Figure 8, 7.1% perfect match on CHARTOM pairs) is a valuable mechanistic insight connecting misleaders to downstream extraction errors.
weaknesses: The headline claim that accuracy on misleading visualizations 'drops to the random baseline' relies on comparing unpaired datasets: the misleading set (n=143) and non-misleading set (n=124) contain different questions, question types, and sources, so difficulty confounds are not controlled. ChartQA (free-text) vs. MCQ datasets is likewise not a like-for-like comparison. The paired evidence (CHARTOM pairs, Experiment 2) is stronger but limited in scale.

Experiment 2 rests on only four visualization pairs (8 charts) from a single prior source; the consistency conclusions, particularly the non-significant results for misrepresentation and 3D effects, are severely underpowered at this sample size.

Many misleader categories have extremely small n (n=1 for missing data, overplotting, pie chart; n=3 for several others), making the per-misleader accuracy claims in Figure 5 fragile and at risk of over-interpretation.

Correction methods are evaluated on only three mid-sized models; there is no evidence the findings (e.g., table-based QA gains of 15.4-19.6 pp, redrawing success rates) generalize to commercial or larger open models.

The real-world subset result is interpreted as parametric knowledge 'protecting' models, but this also raises the concern that some real-world gains reflect answering from memorized facts rather than chart reading - which would inflate real-world accuracy in a way that does not transfer to genuinely novel data, as the authors partly concede but do not quantify.

The manually created MCQs for the new real-world dataset are not validated (e.g., no human accuracy checks or inter-annotator agreement reported), so the correctness and difficulty calibration of the ground-truth labels is unverified.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or variance analysis are reported for the main accuracy comparisons; single runs at temperature 0 are reasonable but the sensitivity of conclusions to prompt phrasing is not examined.

Novelty claims ('first comprehensive study', 'first correction methods') must be read against the cited parallel work (Chen et al., 2025; Pandey and Ottley, 2025; Valentim et al., 2025), which limits how much of the contribution rests on priority rather than the comparative analysis and mitigation trade-off.

strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored problem: robustness of MLLMs to misleading visualizations, which is highly relevant to trustworthy multimodal NLP and disinformation research.

Comprehensive and well-designed empirical study: 19 MLLMs spanning open-weight and commercial families, three complementary experiments (accuracy, Likert-scale consistency, correction methods), and appropriate statistical testing (paired t-tests for Experiment 2, McNemar tests for Experiment 3) rather than relying on raw point estimates alone.

Meaningful methodological contribution through a new dataset of 42 real-world misleading visualizations with MCQs, which creates direct conflicts with parametric knowledge; the paper also carefully distinguishes real-world from synthetic subsets and analyzes parametric-knowledge contamination in Appendix C.

The comparison of six inference-time correction methods is well-motivated, and the analysis goes beyond headline numbers: error analysis of table and axes extraction (Appendices H-I), per-misleader breakdowns, DePlot/MatCha baselines, CoT interactions, and an honest treatment of the trade-off between gains on misleading charts and degradation on non-misleading ones.

Strong transparency and reproducibility: code and data released with licenses specified, prompts provided in appendices, limitations and ethics statements are thoughtful, and related work honestly positions the contribution relative to parallel studies (Chen et al., 2025; Pandey and Ottley, 2025; Valentim et al., 2025) rather than overclaiming.

Key findings are interesting and actionable: MLLM accuracy drops to the random baseline on misleading charts; ranking on ChartQA does not predict robustness to misleaders; table-based QA and visualization redrawing are effective while warnings and axes supplements are not, with a plausible explanation (removing/modifying the visualization matters more than supplementing it).
weaknesses: The evaluation datasets are small (143 misleading and 124 non-misleading instances), which limits statistical power for per-misleader analyses; several misleader categories have only 1-3 instances (e.g., overplotting, missing data reported at 0.0-5.6%), making those conclusions fragile.

Correction-method experiments (Experiment 3) are restricted to only three mid-sized open-weight models, so it is unclear whether the findings (e.g., table-based QA gains of 15-20 pp) generalize to the strongest models like GPT-4o, Gemini-1.5-Pro, or Claude-3.5-Sonnet that were shown to behave differently in Experiment 1.

The random-baseline comparison (25.6% vs 26.4%) is potentially confounded by mixing question types (MCQ, free-text, rank) with different chance levels; the paper does not fully explain how the random baseline is computed for free-text and rank questions.

Manually created MCQs for the new real-world dataset were authored by the paper's authors using CALVI/CHARTOM as references; no inter-annotator agreement, validation study, or human performance on the new subset is reported, leaving open questions about question quality and answerability.

Only inference-time mitigations are explored; no fine-tuning, preference optimization, or detection-then-correct pipeline is evaluated, which somewhat limits the practical impact of the 'protection' framing, especially given the acknowledged need for a misleader detector.

Some findings echo prior or parallel work (Bendeck and Stasko, 2025; Chen et al., 2025), so the novelty rests primarily on the correction-method comparison, trade-off analysis, and real-world subset rather than the vulnerability finding itself.
Minor presentation issues (e.g., a typo in Appendix F, 'it should therefore be applied with caution.t be combined') suggest the manuscript could benefit from another proofreading pass.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-organized empirical study: the paper evaluates 19 MLLMs (open-weight and commercial) across three complementary experiments (accuracy, consistency, and correction), providing the most complete picture to date of MLLM vulnerability to misleading visualizations.

The central empirical claim is well supported: accuracy drops on misleading visualizations are large (up to 34.8 pp; mean accuracy near the random baseline of 25.6%), and are compared against both non-misleading data and reported human accuracy from prior work, situating the results meaningfully.

Methodologically careful for an evaluation paper: statistical significance is assessed appropriately (McNemar test for accuracy changes, paired t-test for Likert consistency), and results are decomposed by misleader type (Table 2, Figure 12), model family, and dataset subset.

The comparison of six inference-time correction methods is a genuine contribution, especially the explicit analysis of the trade-off between gains on misleading charts and degradation on non-misleading ones, which parallel works do not address. The finding that table-based QA and redrawing help while warnings and axes extraction do not is well analyzed.

Strong transparency and reproducibility: code and data are released under clear licenses, prompts are fully specified in the appendix, and the qualitative error analyses (Appendices G–I: table extraction accuracy by misleader, axes extraction analysis) go well beyond typical evaluation papers.

Honest treatment of limitations and confounds, including the parametric-knowledge confound on the real-world subset (Appendix C: GPT4o answers 50% of questions without the image) and the dataset imbalance across misleader categories.
weaknesses: The headline finding — that MLLMs are vulnerable to misleading visualizations — is now largely anticipated by parallel and prior work (Bendeck and Stasko, 2025; Chen et al., 2025; Pandey and Ottley, 2025; Valentim et al., 2025). The genuinely novel contribution is the correction-method comparison, which is narrower in scope.

The evaluation datasets are small (n=143 misleading, n=124 non-misleading) and heavily synthetic (CALVI, CHARTOM), with only 42 real-world instances; the real-world subset is also confounded by parametric knowledge, as the authors themselves show. Per-misleader categories have as few as one instance (overplotting, missing data), making the 0.0% accuracy claims statistically fragile.

The dataset mixes MCQ, free-text, and rank question types, and the misleading/non-misleading sets are not perfectly matched; it is not always clear whether accuracy differences reflect misleader effects or question-type/difficulty differences, and the random baseline (25.6%) is not well justified for the mixed question formats.

Correction methods are evaluated on only three mid-sized open-weight models chosen because they performed below the random baseline in Experiment 1 — a biased sample that limits generalization of the mitigation results to stronger or commercial models.

Experiment 2 rests on only four visualization pairs from a single prior study, and uses a one-sided paired t-test on 19 averaged model ratings; the consistency conclusions are correspondingly thin and partly non-significant.

All corrections are inference-time prompting heuristics; the paper offers no training-based or architectural comparison, and the 'first comparison' framing overstates the delta relative to existing chart-to-table approaches (DePlot/MatCha) tested in the appendix.

The conclusion that correction methods 'often come at the cost of reduced accuracy on non-misleading visualizations' is stated broadly but supported mainly by table-based QA on two models; redrawing shows no significant degradation, so the trade-off framing in the abstract and conclusion is somewhat stronger than the evidence.

strengths: Important and timely problem: robustness of MLLMs to misleading visualizations is a genuine gap in chart-understanding research, with clear societal relevance (disinformation).

Comprehensive empirical scope: 19 MLLMs across open-weight families and commercial models, 17 misleader types spanning three curated datasets plus a newly introduced real-world misleading-visualization dataset (42 MCQs) with released code and data.

Two complementary vulnerability assessments: QA accuracy drops (Experiment 1) and Likert-scale consistency on matched misleading/non-misleading pairs (Experiment 2), with appropriate statistical tests (paired t-tests, McNemar) rather than only raw numbers.

Well-motivated comparison of six inference-time correction methods with an explicit analysis of the trade-off between improving misleading-chart accuracy and preserving non-misleading accuracy, which prior and parallel work does not address.

Thorough error analysis: appendices on table/axes extraction accuracy per misleader, the mediating role of table extraction, parametric-knowledge contamination analysis (Appendix C), DePlot/MatCha baselines, and CoT combinations give the conclusions strong evidential support.

Honest framing: the paper acknowledges that warning-based methods are an upper bound given ground-truth misleader labels, that parallel work exists, and clearly delineates its contributions (real-world subset, correction trade-off) against concurrent benchmarks.
Well-written and clearly organized; figures (e.g., Figure 3 illustrating the correction pipeline, Figures 13-15 extraction error examples) are effective.
weaknesses: Evaluation datasets are small (143 misleading, 124 non-misleading instances; Lauer & O'Brien has only 4 pairs), and misleader categories are highly imbalanced (some with n=1-3), limiting statistical power for per-misleader conclusions and for Experiment 2's four pairwise t-tests (multiple-comparison concerns not addressed).

Correction methods are evaluated on only three mid-sized open-weight MLLMs; it is unclear whether the findings (e.g., table-based QA gains of 15.4-19.6 pp, redraw being safest) generalize to frontier models like GPT-4o or Claude, which are shown to behave differently in Experiment 1.

The headline claim that accuracy drops 'to the level of the random baseline' averages heterogeneous MCQ/free-text/rank question types under one random baseline (25.6%); per-question-type baselines would be more rigorous.

Some correction methods require assumptions that limit practical deployment: chart type and misleader identity are assumed known (warnings), and results would degrade under a realistic misleader-detection pipeline.

Contribution is primarily empirical/benchmarking; the effective methods (table-based QA, redrawing) are existing techniques repurposed, so the novelty is in the comparative analysis rather than methodological innovation.

Minor quality issues: a stray typo ('should therefore be applied with caution.t be combined'), and some claims (e.g., parametric knowledge explaining real-world subset performance) rest on a small analysis (22 questions, one model).
Text-only LLM for table extraction and redrawing (Qwen2.5-7B) is fixed; no sensitivity analysis over the choice of this component.
